Dance Annex — Message Plumbing Map

Every inbound message path, what moves it, and whether it survives an LLM outage. Click any node for detail. Compiled 2026-08-11 from RUNTIMES.md and the event-gate source in dc-canon — maintained since; see the change log at the foot of the page.

LLM fleet runtime — current production

Current production: the lease holder remains Codex. Eleven LLM lanes, including Concierge, run as Hermes VPS crons using Codex / GPT-5.6 Sol; Bookkeeper is deterministic Cloud Run. The installed Bookkeeper Hermes cron is parked outside automatic repair authority. Loop has no scheduled Codex body.

Supervision: deterministic Cloud Run Sentinel remains outside the LLM failure domain. It records versioned incident transitions in Notion and pushes them through private Buzz to Hermes Steward, whose policy permits only narrow mechanical scheduler/MCP repairs. A clean alarm set is not recovery by itself: only Sentinel seeing a post-incident heartbeat may close the loop.

  • Why one worker: one runtime owns each pass, so two agents cannot process the same ticket or write conflicting results.
  • Runtime fencing: the per-lane executor lease prevents the Mac and VPS from owning the same pass; the repair ledger serializes duplicate incident wake-ups.
  • Locking: no Firestore-style cross-runtime lease is required for the first cutover while Codex is the only production LLM writer. Add atomic fencing only if another runtime later receives concurrent write authority.
  • Unchanged machinery: deterministic GCP/event-gate lanes remain in place; Sentinel/SweepWatch remain outside the Concierge failure domain and Notion remains the audit/reconciliation fallback.

🔴 Broken / not yet trusted — fix in this order

  1. RISKRotate mcp-auth-token — it reached a chat transcript.
    Three touchpoints; miss one and every tick 401s silently

    The secret itself, the alarm-mcp redeploy, and both Cloud Scheduler job headers must change together.

  2. GAPNo emergency lane watches email.
    An email-borne emergency waits for the next LLM pass

    SMS has the deterministic 1-min regex lane; email has nothing. Worst case ~2h daytime, ~10h across the overnight Concierge gap. Open since the map was compiled.

  3. WATCHAlarm watchdog is ARMED — and it has already acted wrongly once.
    Re-armed 2026-08-22 behind the occupancy guard; WATCHDOG_ARMED=true, rev alarm-mcp-00053-2rk

    It armed a studio on a person. Studio 693, 2026-08-22, 12:20–12:25 Toronto. Hanano was inside. An alarm fired, she disarmed at 12:20, and the watchdog disarmed and armed away on her at 12:22 and again at 12:24 — she had to disarm three times in five minutes. The same defect hit Sara in 509B the same day. Root cause: in_alarm stays LATCHED TRUE after a human disarm, and executor.py’s pre-command recheck read in_alarm and nothing else — so a person dealing with her own alarm read as “siren still going, nobody has dealt with it”.

    The fix is the occupancy guard — _safe_to_cycle(), every reason NOT to act, checked before any command and never between a disarm and a re-arm. Three questions in order: (1) is the partition still armed — asked first and independently of in_alarm, because somebody disarming is the clearest presence signal this system will ever get; (2) is it still in alarm; (3) is any door open or any motion sensor live. Re-armed the same day behind it.

    State, read live 2026-08-26 03:24Z rather than recalled: flag set on alarm-mcp-00053-2rk, and the panel is quiet — five partitions armed_away, nothing faulted, nothing in_alarm, zero bypassed sensors. Ledgers persist to gs://danceannex-alarm-watchdog, so a cold start cannot forget a suppression.

    Why it still says WATCH. The guard is four days old and has not yet been tested by a real trip with somebody in the room — which is precisely the case it exists for. Kill switch, no redeploy: gcloud run services update alarm-mcp --region us-central1 --remove-env-vars WATCHDOG_ARMED.

  4. DECIDEBypass on a disarmed studio — hold or arm-to-clear?
    Policy call, not code

    Clearing means arming, and a disarmed studio may have someone inside. Junyan's call.

  5. TRICKLELegacy alarm windows migrate one at a time.
    No big-bang panel edit

    Windowed users surface in the Doorman's 7-day table as legacy-window; each is a manual delete → 10-min sync → re-add-as-permanent.

The pipes — what happens without you

Six flows, left to right. Click any hop for its full detail (panel at the foot). Green hops keep running in a token outage; amber hops stop; violet is you.

1 · A renter texts SMS · survives outage until the reply step
Phone.com SMS→ event-gate 1-min poll→ emergency?watchlist names the sender→🚨 on-call SMS+Staff Call Queue simple question?quick-answer card everything elseResponder 30-min→held draft · you release→send engine

Without you: emergencies summon staff and simple questions get answered even in a full token outage. A judgment reply is drafted within ~30 min but nothing sends until a human releases it. The watchlist rebuild is what turns a bare number into a name — LIFE-SAFETY vs UNVERIFIED-distress titling depends on it, so when it goes dark the emergency still summons, just anonymously.

2 · An email arrives business Gmail · the weakest inbound pipe
Business Gmail→ gmail_pull ledger→ Concierge 2-hourly triage→ Notion tickets Personal Gmail→triage-personal-inbox · you drive it→Tasks Inbox · Comms ticket
⚠ GAP: no emergency lane watches email. An email-borne emergency waits for the next LLM pass.

Without you: mail is archived deterministically, but nothing acts on it until an LLM pass — up to ~2h daytime, ~10h overnight. No emergency regex watches this pipe (fix-list item 3). The ledger cron rides flaky GitHub Actions. The personal branch has no deterministic pre-sort at all — it moves only when you sit down and run the triage skill.

3 · A message goes out every outbound email/SMS · human-gated by design
agent drafts a queue row→ Pending Review · you release→ send engine 1-min poll · v18 guards→ renter template cardsReceptionist hourly :00→Pending Review · same valve

Without you: nothing customer-facing sends — your release is the valve. The engine refuses malformed rows instead of sending them (single sender identity, Invariant J unthreaded-reply guard); failures flip to Error + alert email, never silent. Scheduled FBS sends (HTA/EOB/AVA) flow once queued.

4 · A booking becomes access Skedda → alarm codes · ⚠ upstream data is broken
Skedda ⚠ cookie→ fbs-monitor 15-min rebuild→ Doorman 04:00 + ~06:00→ PIN digits — staff→ HTA with code

Without you: the board rebuilds and the Doorman preflights access 7 days out, checks arm state overnight, and proposes (never executes) code retirements. PIN digits stay human — the panel masks them. Everything here reads through the broken Skedda cookie (fix-list item 1) until it is reseeded.

5 · Something breaks watchers watching workers · deterministic where it counts
fbs-watch 15-min→ Slack #desk-status Sentinel + Watchman hourly→ miss → SMS desk-loop + invariants→ alarm-watchdog ARMED→ watchdog log overnight reports→ your morning surfaces

Without you: a fleet outage reaches Slack deterministically; a missed agent run reaches your phone. The alarm watchdog is ARMED and acts on its own — its four lanes are pipe 6 below. Everything else lands on the Night Watch / Fixer pages for your morning.

6 · The alarm handles itself alarm-mcp · every 60s · deterministic · ARMED since 2026-08-22
siren?3 min of siren — let it scare→⛔ anyone inside? guard→disarm + re-arm, that partition only→2 strikesa person bypass? (:15)clean cycle restores the sensor→2 strikesa person — door is likely open any trouble?the sorter — 5 ways out→SMS you|Maintenance row|ignore (listed)|unknown → STILL a row tamper?ticket · any hour→SMS Stefan · daytime · ×2→then YOU→clears → row resolves itself

Without you: a tripped siren clears and re-arms itself (max twice, and never with a person inside — the ⛔ guard checks arm state, in_alarm, and open/motion sensors before any command); a stuck bypass is restored; every panel trouble lands somewhere a human can see it — the sorter’s default is now file a ticket, not silence; a tamper runs its own ticket→Stefan→you loop and closes its own row. All deterministic: it keeps working in a full token outage. On the 🚥 Run Monitor since 2026-08-26 — it stamps its own Self-heartbeat every 5 min (row alarm-watchdog (Cloud Run), stale after 15, window 00–24), outside the arm switch, so a stale row means the service is dead rather than merely disarmed. This entry previously read “not on the Sentinel roster, deliberately — not an LLM agent with runs to miss”. That was wrong: determinism is not liveness, the board already carries deterministic jobs, and the only liveness proof was a log line nobody but an agent reads.

    Why. A renter often gets a text and a charge or invoice for the same event. They lived on two tabs and drifted apart (one sent, the other forgotten).

    Route change. A Pending Review queue row and an open Charge/Invoice Action row pair when the Action names the reply ([PAY-LINK-MQ:<id>]), the draft's DECK-INVOICE-V1 invoice id is on the Action, or they share one Customer Care / Sales ticket with exactly one waiting text and one open money row (anything else: no pair). The Messages card shows "With this text: Charge $X". A reply with its own invoice shows the real pay.danceannex.ca link in place of {invoice_link} (KV only, no Stripe call), Send finalizes it, /api/bundle/mark writes INVOICED ... (BUNDLE-V1 MQ <id>) on the Action (it checks the pair again server side), then the text releases. A reply with no invoice reads "Charge $X + send": the press shows the Charges tab's own preview, the second press runs /api/charge/run with bundle_queue (no separate pay-link text, no fill; the short link comes back for the reply), then the text releases. The Deck cannot bill the row: the card offers "Send text only" and the row returns to Charges. Mark fails: the text still goes and a toast says to check the row on Charges before billing it. Manual, relay, booking-change and engine-blocked cards never bundle.

    Charges tab flags "New card added" when a renter saves a card after a Deck decline; a new card gets its own pay keydeck · route · src/invoice-card-charge.js (payKey), src/new-card.js (recordDecline, onCardEvent, verifyStripeSignature), src/open-invoices.js (markNewCards), src/index.js (POST /stripe-webhook, deckSlackDm), sources/deck.html (cardBtnHtml, liveNudge, Charges poll) · deck-app

    Junyan: “d49 "yes"; d51 "really useful whenever a card is declined. We often have a small window of time to make the charge so we should take advantage" (2026-10-28)”

    Why. A re-press within 24 h of a decline replayed the decline even with a new card, and nobody knew when a renter had saved a new card.

    Route change. The Charge card pay key is now deck-card-pay-<invoice>-<card id>: the same card on the same invoice still replays Stripe's first answer, a new card is a fresh try. A decline from the Deck press is remembered in KV (cardfail:<invoice>, 30 days). Stripe posts customer.updated (a new default card) to POST /stripe-webhook (signature checked with STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET); if an open Deck invoice of that customer was declined on another card, the Deck pushes a live "charges" nudge to open pages and DMs Junyan and Ela on Slack once per invoice and card (NEW_CARD_ALERT_DISABLED=true stops the DM). The Charges read marks that row "New card added: declined on •••• X, now •••• Y. Not charged yet." and its button names the new card. The Charges tab re-reads Stripe every 45 s while open. Nothing here charges: the press is still Junyan's or Ela's own (d48).

    Failure mode. No STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET: the webhook answers 503 and the marker still appears on the next 45 s read. A bad signature answers 400 and does nothing. A decline Stripe made itself (not a Deck press) counts only when the default card was created after it. A Slack failure leaves no DM record, so the next card event tries the DM again.

    A Stripe draft invoice can bill a Skedda series one date per linestripe-mcp · tool · services/stripe-mcp/stripe_mcp/server.py, services/stripe-mcp/tests/test_stripe_mcp.py, library/invoicing.md, deck-app open-invoices.js · desk-correspondence #1432

    Junyan: “43 yes (2026-10-28)”

    Why. A Skedda series has one booking id for every date. A draft invoice line named only that id, so the Deck read it as billing the whole series and took every later date off "To charge".

    Tool change. stripe-mcp create_draft_invoice lines take an optional occurrence (the date's local start, e.g. 2026-11-03T19:00), stored as line metadata skedda_occurrence in the Deck's own format (2026-11-03T19:00:00-05:00). The same booking_id may repeat on several lines only with distinct dates; a repeated date, or the same booking with and without a date, is refused before any write. The Deck (deck-app PR for d43) clears only the dated rows. Paying is unchanged: each date is marked paid in Skedda with settle_charged_occurrence (library/invoicing.md § Series).

    Tool surface. - Keys (only while the Gmail tab shows and nothing is being typed): - J/K (or the arrow keys in the list) move the highlight; in a thread they open the next or previous one. - Enter or O opens the highlighted thread. U or Esc goes back to the list. - E marks Done and opens the next thread. - Z undoes a Send in its countdown, else the last Done (10 s). - ⌘K opens a list of every action with its key, filtered by typing; Enter runs one. - Done: a Deck-side mark in the DeckLive Gmail cache (gmail:done:<key>, shared by every login, like the seen marks), set through POST /api/gmail/done (undo removes it). Gmail is not touched: the grant stays read only. - Empty list: "Inbox zero. Nothing is waiting on you."

    Guards (review). - The mark stores the newest email the person had in front of them (sent by the page), so one that came in after is never hidden unseen. - A saved Done drops the thread from every page held, older pages too. - Undo waits for the Done to reach the server first. - Enter on a focused row opens that row. - ⌘K toggles the list, and Esc always closes it. - Z after the 10 s does nothing.

    Failure mode. A Done that cannot be saved puts the thread back in the list and says so. Done hides a thread only in the Deck, so it still shows in Gmail.

    The Send Engine can write the Queue and Run Monitor through event-gate's Notion door (off until switched on)Send Engine · route, failure · send-engine PR https://github.com/junyanboon/send-engine/pull/62 (v44, StoreRouter.gs, notionFetchOnce_), desk-correspondence PR https://github.com/junyanboon/desk-correspondence/pull/1287 (the door), fast store slice 5b, d122 · desk-correspondence #1297

    Why. The Send Engine writes the Message Queue and Run Monitor straight into Notion, so event-gate's fast store only learns those writes at the daily copy. Sending the same call through event-gate's Notion door keeps the store in step (fast store slice 5b).

    Route change. New in v44 and off by default: with the router off, every Notion call goes exactly as in v43. Once Junyan switches a table on (storeRouterQueueOn, storeRouterRunMonitorOn, Script Property STORE_ROUTER_LIVE), the engine sends that table's row creates and its patches of rows it has already seen to the door at /store/v1/notion/, which makes the Notion call with event-gate's token. Queries go to the door only for a table event-gate has flipped. Page reads never go to the door (d113): the last checks before a send read Notion. Comments, blocks, SweepWatch.gs and other tables stay on Notion. Door calls use the v43 event-gate pause.

    Failure mode. If the door refuses a call (busy, off, store down, unknown row), the engine makes the same call to Notion itself, then files a touched report (/store/v1/notion/touched, kept as STORE_TOUCHED_<id> properties, at most 300, sent after the heartbeat) so event-gate re-reads that page into the store. A create that the door may have sent (no answer, Notion's own 5xx, a timeout) is never resent: the engine stops on it with "NOT resent", the same as a Notion timeout today, so no message goes twice. InsuranceIntake.gs keeps its own one-shot Queue create on Notion and reports it as touched. Off switch: storeRouterOff in the editor.

    Why. The robot tables are moving from Notion to event-gate's own Postgres store one table at a time. Each move starts by copying the Notion table into the store. This is the tool that does it.     Tool change. store_copy.py (run by hand inside the event-gate container) copies one mapped Notion data source into its store table: insert or update by Notion page id, never delete, keep Notion's edit times, archived and trash flags and the raw properties. A --dry-run reads and reports and writes nothing. Each run prints one report line (seen, inserted, updated, unchanged, failed, calls, why it stopped, row count and checksum) and records it in store_copy_runs. First table: Live Tests (live_tests, migration 003). It shares the robots' Notion line (notion_http): its own cap is 0.25 calls a second (the line is 2.7), at most 200 calls a run by default (1000 hard cap), and it will not start between 01:00 and 11:00 UTC unless forced. The nightly store backup now counts rows inside the same database snapshot pg_dump uses, so the restore drill stays exact once tables take writes.

    Failure mode. The copy stops cleanly and can be rerun to carry on when it hits its call budget, a Notion rate limit, a line wait over 10 s, 01:00 UTC, or another copy of the same table (exit 3); a Notion or store error stops it with exit 1. Every finished 100-row batch is already saved. A page whose values do not fit is kept raw and counted as failed. If the backup's snapshot session fails, that night's backup fails with no archive (as a failed pg_dump did before) and the Sentinel sees the stale record. Off switch: do not run the tool; the tables it fills are read by nothing.

    Fallback Analyst and Timekeeper stop mistaking a registered trigger for a live writerThe Analyst, The Timekeeper · failure · FIX + POLICY CORRECTION

    Moved here on 2026-10-02 from day-sheet PR #1, which was never merged.

    The failure: the Codex fallback Analyst saw the Claude trigger still registered and enabled, treated that registry row as proof that Claude was actively working, and stopped at the collision gate even though the Claude fleet was quota-blocked. The forward-looking IPR went stale or missing. The same false-positive gate could prevent the Timekeeper from repairing an absent run.

    The corrected gate: registration and enabled state are schedule intent, not active-work evidence. A fallback run now yields only to concrete post-slot evidence: an in-progress run monitor, a matching runtime process, or a completed report written for that slot. This changes no trigger state and does not permit overlapping writers.

    The ownership and billing rails: the Analyst owns forward-looking today/tomorrow IPRs; the Timekeeper exclusively owns retrospective overtime. For direct bookings, the Timekeeper corrects source lag first; once the adjusted overage meets the 17-minute flag threshold, it bills the complete 15-minute blocks and leaves any final 1–14 minutes unbilled as the grace remainder. Junyan’s example is explicit: 36 adjusted minutes is two billed 15-minute blocks plus 6 grace minutes; Ish’s corrected 29-minute example is one billed block plus 14 grace minutes. Booking duration and held suggested amount must describe the same billed block total. No charge, settlement, message release, or trigger enable/disable is part of this repair.

    Correction during review: an earlier draft incorrectly described one 30-minute block. It never reached main. The live Timekeeper, SOP, regression check, and both review branches were corrected before the next scheduled run; the public Terms’ 15-minute-increment wording now agrees with the operational block size.

    What a 429 blocked. Only the two read polls. /api/claims threw, so the page kept its last-known claims from localStorage and showed no new claims by anyone else until 00:00Z. /api/booking-updates threw, so every booking card lost its update chip (pending / decision / done) and the updater showed a status error.     The fix. src/kv_index.js: each key family keeps one JSON index of key names (index:claims, index:bu:<day>). A poll is one get for the index plus one get per key, so it draws on the 100,000 read allowance. Writers append to the index after storing the value; readers drop keys that expired. KV has no atomic append, so the index rebuilds itself from a real list when missing or older than an hour — about 48 lists a day for both families, well under the cap. Test: five polls, a claim, five more polls, an expiry — exactly one list. 46 tests pass. Live since 22:08Z (Junyan deployed; version 0a625515). One gap found after the first deploy: the rebuild itself calls list, the very call KV refuses for the rest of the day, so the first poll still failed. Second commit 9cc49e6 catches the refusal and answers from the stored index or an empty one. Tail at 22:15Z: /api/claims and /api/booking-updates both Ok, logging kv index rebuild skipped … limit exceeded. 52 tests.

The worst carries three codes in one title, one of them a DOOR code the row itself says is “still in a stranger’s hands”.

    No deterministic writer ever did this. Every title-building call in services/ was read: the only code-shaped field a Python lane puts in a title is Message Code, a message identifier. Five LLM lanes did it; five LLM lanes still run. So the enforcement moved out of the prompt and into the writer. lane_common.scrub_code redacts any 4-digit group written next to the word for it — code / pin / passcode / digits, either order, both halves of a rotation — to ••••, and BOTH shared row writers (lane_common.action_row and booking_sweep.residue) run it over every title, basis and note. A rule an LLM can ignore became a property of the pipe.

    It REDACTS, it never refuses. These rows are urgent access problems — somebody is about to stand at a locked door. Dropping the row to protect the digits would trade a leak for a stranding, and “never silence a real stall” outranks it. The row survives and still says what is wrong; only the digits go.

    Tuned against the whole archive, not against intuition: all 1223 real titles and bases, 10 changed, 0 false positives. A date (2026-09-05), a time (19:30), a studio (509A) and a booking id (120309286) all survive, because a leak is only a 4-digit group that is not part of a longer number or a date AND sits beside the word for what it is. The first draft of this guard would have redacted the year in every residue key — which is exactly the false positive that made ticket 124 report a code-carrying row that never carried one.

    2. Gate 2 was still silent, and that is the same defect one layer over. PR #72 gave the identity ladder and the tag strip their log lines and left the MOST COMMON outcome invisible: an established platform renter — card, phone, working code — clears at gate 2 on every pass, never reaches the ladder, and carries no desk tag to strip. All six platform bookings in the 2026-09-09 window (Natascha M ×2, Best O., Jia L., Sol R. via Peerspace; Matthew Jadd via Tagvenue) are exactly that shape, so #72 would have proved nothing. Found by reading who was actually coming, not by re-reading the code.

    The lesson worth keeping. A rule that only exists in a prompt is a rule that gets ignored, and the evidence was ten rows old before anyone looked. When the same rule is broken by five different actors, stop rewriting the rule and change what the writer will accept.

    The defect is a disagreement, not a typo. The reply path matched only a Gmail web URL’s #all/<id> fragment. The Deck’s own reader, gmailHex(), matches a 16-hex id preceded by /, :, - or whitespace — so gmail:1a078b… is a valid Source Email as far as the Deck is concerned, and its edit placeholder says only “Gmail link, hex-id form”. Two components read one field by different rules. Whoever pasted that value was following the wider rule.

    What changed. The engine moved to the wider rule: both #all/<id> and a bare gmail:<id> now parse. The id in the receipt form is a real Gmail MESSAGE id, and the message→thread resolution already sitting below the parse handles exactly that, so nothing new was needed to use it. Anything matching neither shape still errors — an unrecognised link must stop the row for a human, never quietly become a new out-of-thread email.

    Not fixed, and worth a decision. The disagreement is only closed from one side. The Deck still accepts shapes the engine will refuse if a third one ever appears, and no writer validates the field at entry. The durable fix is one stated format for Source Email that both sides cite.

Try reducing the rate of data transfer. The URL is Notion’s, so the error reads like a Notion rate limit. It is Google’s. Apps Script caps UrlFetch data received at 100MB per day on a consumer account, and thedanceannex@gmail.com is one. Once the day’s allowance is gone every fetch throws, so the engine dies at its first call and sends nothing until midnight Pacific.

    The defect. queryReadyRows_ asked Notion for Status = Ready to Send and nothing else. main polls every minute, so a message queued for tomorrow came back in FULL on every one of those polls — all ~30 properties — and processRow_ discarded it again against its Send After. A row queued a day ahead was read about 1,400 times before it was ever sent. The scheduling test existed; it just sat on the wrong side of the wire.

    Why it broke now and not months ago. Two quantities grew past a fixed cap. The queue got deeper — 14 rows sat Ready to Send when this was measured, most waiting on future Send After times — and the rows got fatter, because Reasoning now accumulates an edit and error history alongside a full Message Body. 14 rows at a few KB, 1,440 times, is ~70MB before a single dispatch-time page read. An FBS day with 30 queued rows clears 100MB on its own.

    What changed. The Send After test moved to the server: the filter is now Status = Ready to Send AND (Send After is empty OR on_or_before now). Almost every poll now returns nothing. Behaviour is unchanged by construction — this is the same test processRow_ already applied at dispatch, and the client-side check stays exactly where it was and stays authoritative. Cadence untouched: still one minute, still 1-minute send resolution.

    The safety, which is the point of the shape. A malformed filter would have Notion answer 400 and stop every send — strictly worse than the bandwidth problem it fixes. So the query catches a rejection and falls back to the old wide filter, which is always accepted, and logs that it did. A second failure mode is quieter: a filter Notion ACCEPTS but reads differently than intended could hide a row that is due. testDueFilter() exists for that one — it runs both filters against live rows, applies the client test to the wide result, and prints PASS only if every due row survives the narrow filter. It sends nothing and writes nothing. Run it from the editor after any change to dueFilter_().

    Also added. Every Notion response now logs its byte count. Apps Script reports nothing about this quota until it is spent, so until now the only evidence of the ceiling was hitting it.

    Measured, 2026-09-07 09:10 Toronto. testDueFilter() run by hand in the editor — clasp run fails on this project (NOT_FOUND; no API-executable deployment), so this check needs a human. Wide query 68,148 bytes, narrow query 172 bytes, 13 ready rows, 0 due, 0 returned, PASS. 68KB × 1440 polls = 98MB against a 100MB cap — the engine was spending 98% of its daily allowance on rows it discarded, which is why one extra queued row tipped it over on 09-06 and not before. The narrow query costs 0.25MB a day.

    The board invented a person: arm events now dedup on STATE, not the clockFAILURE MODE · fbs-monitor f191a8f1 · LIVE NEXT REBUILD

    Spotted by Junyan on the Alarms tab, 2026-09-05 23:1x Toronto. Studio 509A showed a disarm at 18:53 with no name, sitting between Simona Horova’s 18:40 disarm and her 19:52 arm. Alarm.com’s own portal and its PastEvents export have no 18:53 event at all — only those two, both hers. The board made it up.

    Two feeds, one event, and the second copy has no name. /door-history (the websocket) carries the actor and the true second. /arm-history (the panel ledger) carries no actor and stamps the event at its own watchdog tick, so it always lands late. The builder kept a panel event only when no door event of the same studio+kind sat within 8 minutes — a window sized off a measured 1-6 minute lag (2026-08-20, 13:26:24 → 13:29).

    What broke it. The listener was down 18:45:53–18:52:52 and the ledger’s writer stalled with it. Its first tick after recovery, 54 seconds later, wrote her 18:40:07 disarm at 18:53:46 — 13m38s late, past the window. The panel copy survived as a “backstop”, and since the ledger names nobody the page printed no name on this source. fetch_arm_history also hardcodes remote: False, so a phantom always renders as an in-person arrival — it reads as a second body in a room that had one. Any fixed window has this bug: the lag is normal tick lag PLUS however long the writer stalled, which is unbounded.

    The fix — state, not elapsed time. panel_backstop() replaces the inline window check. arrival means the partition is disarmed; departure means armed. A panel event that restates the state the timeline is already in is a restatement, not an event — you cannot disarm an already-disarmed panel — so it drops however late it lands. An event that flips the state is one the socket genuinely lost, and it survives.     Asked. Junyan, 2026-09-05, after Nabil Fairbairn’s Oct 16 went in as an orphan: “Can we fix it so that edit-booking has a way to extend a series? This happens all the time so it’s a needed function.”

    The hole. There was no supported way to add a date to a series that already exists. edit_booking changes one occurrence’s when/where and cannot touch the repeat rule. create_booking’s series-first guard refuses a loose booking matching an existing series’ title, space and time-of-day. That left two bad exits: force it with allow_unbatched_repeat=True, leaving an orphan the series can no longer move or reprice as a unit, or delete and rebuild the series, which mints new booking ids and loses paid/unpaid state on dates the renter already settled. Live case: Nabil’s WCS practice group, Studio 693 Friday series 120370013 (Sep 11 / Sep 25 / Oct 2). He asked for Friday Oct 16; it went in as standalone 120389575, deliberately left as-is.

    Built. add_occurrence(booking_id, on_date) — the everyday “can you add another one?”: pushes UNTIL out to that date and excludes every other date the extension would create, so exactly one booking appears. extend_series(booking_id, until, skip_dates) — the renewal: runs a whole series on longer with holidays skipped. Both are the mirror of release_occurrence, which drops a date from a series; these add dates to it. Both dry-run by default.

    Why extending beats rebuilding. Only the UNTIL= token is rewritten. DTSTART, EXDATE and every other RRULE component (FREQ, INTERVAL, BYDAY, BYSETPOS, BYMONTHDAY) are preserved verbatim — the same discipline _set_exdates already follows, because a rebuild from parsed parts would have to round-trip every component perfectly and anything dropped silently changes which dates the series falls on. Occurrences the series already has keep their ids, prices and payment status. add_occurrence refuses an off-pattern date, a date inside the existing span (pointing at release_occurrence(restore=True) when it is an exception), and an unexpandable recurrence shape. 11 new tests; 42 pass.

    Failure mode found in passing. find_booking’s no-date sweep was ±400 days — about 26 months against Skedda’s documented 16-month per-request cap, so it answered HTTP 422 every single time it was called. That path is not new code: release_occurrence(restore=True) uses it, so restoring a released occurrence has been broken and would have 422’d on every attempt. Now swept in 200-day chunks, nearest dates first. No test — the suite is offline-only with no HTTP fixtures.

    Live. skedda-cli fd4d87c pushed; ./deploy.sh put service skedda-mcp-00065-ldq and job skedda-refresh on the same image. Verified by tools/list against the hosted endpoint: both tools present. Dry-run against the real series reads until_before 2026-10-02 → until_after 2026-10-16, dates_added ['2026-10-16'], dates_skipped ['2026-10-09'], existing EXDATE Sep 18 preserved.

    What happened. Jia L. booked twice through Peerspace — Sun Sep 6 and Sat Sep 12. Two replies were drafted, one per booking, and both were delivered into the Sep 12 thread.     Why. Peerspace and Tagvenue mint one relay address per BOOKING. The relay is the whole routing decision — it is what puts a reply in one thread rather than the other. Each queue row carried its own correct relay on Reply To, written by the Greeter. But the send engine read the recipient off the Artist relation’s Email rollup and never off the row (Code.gs readRow_ / sendEmail_, commented “the row’s Email rollup is the authoritative recipient on BOTH paths”). One card holds one Email. Two bookings, one card, one address — so the second relay had been found, filed, and then thrown away at dispatch.

The card-creating fix of 2026-09-04 (greeter_sweep.ensure_platform_artist, written because Jia’s row had a relay but no card and so no send door) stores one relay per guest per platform. It gave the engine a door and, in the same stroke, made every later booking by that guest point at the first booking’s thread. The Registrar’s platform_relay_artist reads the same single Email, so its gate-1 auto-send — a live carve-out — had the same misroute waiting on Jia’s Sep 12 booking.

    The fix. On the Email lane only: when the row carries a parseable Reply To, that address is the recipient; the Artist rollup is the fallback. Blank or malformed Reply To behaves exactly as before, so every non-platform row is untouched. The self-address guard runs on the final recipient, so a relay that resolves to one of ours is still refused rather than sent. SMS is not in the path. The Artist card keeps its job as the identity anchor — it just stops being the address book for per-booking relays.

Both read Google-side storage. The error says storage. main fails on the lock; platformMirrorTick fails on the flag read. That is the whole fault.

    The fix — v23. Not a retry around the run; a retry around those two calls. props_() now returns a retrying wrapper — one choke point covering 76 property reads across six files, and the only PropertiesService reference in the project. All five entry points (main, notifyInbound, docIntakeTick, platformMirrorTick, sameDayTick) now take the lock via takeScriptLock_(). Two retries, 1s then 3s. Four of the five had the same latent flaw and had simply not failed yet.

    What still fails loudly, deliberately. A missing script property throws on the first attempt, unchanged. A permission error throws on the first attempt, no retry. A storage outage that outlives the retries still throws, still fails the fire and still emails — per the house rule never to silence an alert that might be a real stall. A dispatch engine that stops silently is worse than one that is noisy. Only the blips go quiet.

    Verification. Nine cases in a Node sandbox with stubbed Google services, all passing: recovery after one and after two blips; persistent outage still throws; lock-already-held returns null with no retry; healthy path takes exactly one call; permission error throws immediately; property read recovers; missing property still throws; backoff measured at 1000ms then 3000ms.     Junyan ran the ten-second test the 2026-08-09 alarm reconciliation asked for. He typed the known-dead code 2578 on the local panel. “There is no code when I type 2578 on the local panel.” The panel did not accept it.

    What was at stake. Deleting an Alarm.com user does not release its code from the panel slots — the number survives as an ownerless reservation, which is what produces the red form error “Code is already being used by these users: (4 Locations)” with no user named. 520 Artist rows carry such a code. The open question was binary: if an orphaned slot still disarms, then ~520 working all-studio codes belong to nobody, appear in no audit, and sit in former renters’ text messages — a standing access hole. If it does not, the slots block reuse and nothing else.

    Answer: it does not disarm. An orphaned slot is a uniqueness reservation only. So §4 of that report is cosmetic, not urgent: no former renter can enter with an old code, and the ~520 rows are a capacity and tidiness problem. Recorded in archive/REPORT-alarm-code-reconciliation-2026-08-09.md §4, which had carried the instruction “Do not size any cleanup before it.” That block is now lifted.

    Scope of the evidence, stated plainly: one code, on one panel. 2578 was Nabil Fairbairn’s, owner 245317997, deleted. The deletion mechanism is uniform across users, so the result is expected to hold for every orphan. It is not proof that all ~520 behave the same way.

    Still parked, and not blocked by the keypad: actually deleting the slots needs a panel-side code export per system. No tool in this runtime can enumerate or remove a code slot — every write tool targets a user_id, and orphans have none. Watch for: the only live cost of leaving them is that those numbers cannot be reissued, so a provisioning failure that blames capacity should look here first.

By the time the board rebuilt, the card’s canonical EOB slot had become end−15m = 13:15. Gap: 30 minutes against a 5-minute join window (abs(...) <= 300). The sent row fell out of the match, matches came back empty, and _dispatch_pill published MISSING.

    The AVA pill on the same booking was correct — expected 12:00−2h = 10:00, row Send After = 14:00Z = 10:00 ET, exact hit, Sent, no pill.     The fix is not a wider window. No window survives a booking that moves after its message is scheduled — widening only changes which extension breaks it, and a loose window mis-attaches a row between two bookings, which is the failure the 5 minutes exists to prevent. The real bug is that a failed time match was being read as proof of absence. It is not. apply_message_dispatch() now publishes nothing when nothing joins but a terminal row (Sent / Will Not Send / Error) exists for the same Artist + Studio + kind — the same fail-safe the function already applies when the relation join is incomplete (“absence is UNKNOWN, never MISSING”). Terminal statuses are now one constant, DISPATCH_TERMINAL_STATUSES, instead of the same three strings written twice.

    What MISSING still catches. A kind with no row at all is still absent and still fires. A live row that misses its slot by half an hour is a genuine scheduling fault and still fires — only finished work suppresses the claim. And a terminal row cannot mute a pill the queue still owes: a replacement that joins is chosen first, so a stale Error beside a fresh Pending Review never speaks for the booking. The cost is honest and narrow: where one Artist + Studio has two bookings the same day and a sent row matches only one, the other now stays quiet instead of claiming absence it cannot prove.

    ⚠️ The line rang BECAUSE it reported zero errors. progress_level() reads counters first — a trouble-named counter holding zero is the strongest possible statement that nothing went wrong, so it must never be what sets off the alarm — then scans whatever text is LEFT as prose. So the counter pass matched nothing, stripped nothing, and the counters survived intact into the prose scan, where error and failed ring the bell.

    What changed — the parser, not the three routes. The other candidate was normalising the three routes to emit JSON summaries. Rejected: the routes are not the bug, the parser’s blind spot is — and route number four would open it again. Bare word N is how a human writes a summary; the parser has to be able to read one. What the routes report is unchanged — the counts are useful, and _PROGRESS_ALARM_WORDS was neither widened nor trimmed.

    The strip is narrow on purpose. A blanket word N removal would chew the middle out of a real complaint — timed out 5 times would lose timed out to the out 5 match and go silently quiet, which is the same disease pointed the other way. Only trouble-named keys are removed, and by then a trouble-named counter has already rung if it held anything, so what comes out is always a zero.

The thermostat commands themselves are naturally idempotent — sending “cool to 23.0°C” twice lands in the same place. A lost pass on a per-minute lane self-heals in 60 seconds anyway, so the retry buys ~30s of recovery in exchange for concurrent passes. alarm-watchdog already overlaps by design (attemptDeadline 360s against a 60s period). Both were set back to retryCount=0 the same night (Junyan: “yes go ahead”) — verified by reading the full retryConfig back, since the API omits retryCount entirely when it is 0 rather than sending zero: the same absent-means-false trap RUNTIMES.md already records for enabled on the trigger listing.     ⚠️ Backoff does NOT have to fit inside attemptDeadline. An earlier reading of this was wrong: attemptDeadline bounds a single HTTP attempt, not the retry sequence (maxRetryDuration: 0s = unlimited total). The constraint that actually matters is the gap to the next scheduled fire — which is exactly what the two per-minute jobs above violate.

    Lesson worth banking: a watchdog with no retries turns every upstream blip into a fleet-wide alarm. The alert text said “nothing is watching the fleet” and that was true for 60 minutes — but the cause was one unretried HTTP request, not a dead lane. Read the scheduler’s own attempt record before believing a service is down; it distinguishes “never asked”, “asked and refused”, and “asked and crashed”, and only the third is the service’s fault.

Cosmetic, but it makes a severity-filtered log read as a permanent fire and hides real errors in the noise.

    The fix. The three loose rules now demand the family’s own phrasing rather than its topic: review request|review ask|positive-feedback review, Additional Time Charges or the T1 (…) — N additional time, shape, and alarm check-in / ^ALARM-T….   • 2026-08-31

    Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol) lane for Process Studio Tickets — built, proven, then NOT adopted LANE PARKED

    Verdict (Junyan, 2026-08-31): parked, not adopted. The lane works — everything below was proven against live data — but the economics did not justify switching. Measured across 22 real ticket-processing runs in the local transcripts, the median run costs ~65k output and ~16.9M cache-read tokens over ~80 assistant turns. Crucially, only 15% of a run’s tokens land before the first write (mean 21%): reads and writes interleave the whole way, so there is no clean read-heavy front half to hand to a cheaper engine. A “Codex scouts, Claude executes” hybrid would save ~15% for real handoff friction, and a full switch means giving up the interactive flow. Since the 16.9M is dominated by cache reads — roughly a tenth the price of fresh input — the dollar saving is far smaller than the token count suggests. Do not re-litigate this without new numbers. The config below is left in place and safe; nothing routes through it.

    Why: Claude subscription tokens were running short and the ticket pass still had to happen. The process-studio-tickets skill already existed in Codex at ~/.codex/skills/process-studio-tickets/SKILL.md — same thin pointer that fetches the live Notion runtime page each run — but Codex had no Notion and no Gmail connector, so it died on step 1.

    What changed: two MCP servers added to ~/.codex/config.toml. notion → hosted https://mcp.notion.com/mcp, OAuth completed. gmail-business → the same local stdio server Claude uses (npx -y @gongrzhe/server-gmail-autoauth-mcp with GMAIL_CREDENTIALS_PATH=/Users/jboon/.gmail-mcp/business-credentials.json), so no re-auth. Backup of the prior config at ~/.codex/config.toml.bak-1787855836.

    The failure mode that cost the time: every Gmail tool call in codex exec came back user cancelled MCP tool call. Not an auth failure and not a timeout — the server answered fine when driven directly over JSON-RPC. Codex was raising an approval elicitation (mcp_tool_call_approval_…) per tool call, and headless exec auto-cancels any prompt it cannot show. Fix: default_tools_approval_mode = "auto" on the server block. Valid values are auto, prompt, writes, approve — strings scraped from the binary suggested allow, which is wrong and fails the whole config load with unknown variant. Set on both gmail-business and notion; Notion reads were passing unprompted (its read tools carry readOnlyHint) but writes — the actual ticket creation — would have hit the same cancel.

    The landmine, and the reason a run can look clean while doing nothing: on this server label:"Sales - Booking Request" silently returns an empty result — no error, no warning. It reads exactly like “no tickets waiting.” The first rehearsal reported both queues empty; they were not. Both refusals therefore consumed the two-attempt cap without one disarm/re-arm command being sent. Every later pass emitted bypass_stuck and stopped retrying. Attempts move to post-execution accounting and persist only on acted=True, ok=True. The durable ledger is versioned to v2 and discards the old counters once because no v1 counter can prove a real cycle occurred. A bypass that survives two completed cycles now texts on-call once per episode; delivery is durable across cold starts, resets when the sensor clears, and a failed text retries next pass. Commits a59cf42 + 796a6ee, image alarm:0829-796a6ee, revision alarm-mcp-00060-qgq; 277 tests.

Scheduler recorded HTTP 200 even though no bypass decision ran. Busy now returns HTTP 503, and this one job has exactly one retry after 10 seconds (retryCount=1, minBackoffDuration=10s). That is long enough for the ordinary tick to leave and bounded enough not to turn a panel action into an open-ended retry loop.

    Production proof, ordinary schedule: the unchanged 23:45 fire emitted [watchdog] armed=True bypass=True :: bypass_restore:Studio 509A, called it Attempt 1 of 2, and completed acted=True ok=True. The durable v2 ledger then contained exactly 101222561-1: 1; the old refusals were not resurrected. At 23:54 Toronto, nine minutes after execution, Alarm.com no longer reported Sensor Bypassed (Studio 509A Door): all five studios were armed away and all 18 sensors needed no attention.     The gate’s last two plaintext credentials move into Secret Manager FIX

    What changed: NOTION_TOKEN and GATE_PATH_TOKEN were the only credentials on event-gate still stored as literal environment values — readable by anyone with console or gcloud describe access, while the other seven already came from Secret Manager.     The secret that would have broken it. A notion-token secret already existed (created 2026-08-16, wired to nothing) — and it was 51 bytes: the 50-char token plus a trailing newline, which Python’s http.client rejects outright as a header value. Pointing the service at it would have killed every Notion read on the gate. Caught by hashing before deploying rather than after: sha256(secret) did not match sha256(live env value), but sha256(secret trimmed) did. A clean 50-byte v2 was minted and the service pins :2, not :latest, so v1 cannot return. Same disease as the 2026-08-16 mcp-auth-token incident (267 failed panel reads); the lesson generalises to byte-check every secret against the known-working value before a service depends on it.

    Deploy trap, new and worth remembering: gcloud refuses to convert an env var from a literal to a secret reference in place — Cannot update environment variable [NOTION_TOKEN] to the given type because it has already been set with a different type. The fix is --remove-env-vars and --update-secrets in the same command (removals apply before updates inside one revision). Splitting it into two commands would be a self-inflicted outage: the gate fails closed, so a revision without GATE_PATH_TOKEN 404s every route including the every-minute emergency poller — precisely the 2026-08-15 shape. The failed first attempt changed nothing (Cloud Run rejects the whole revision), so the retry was free.

    Verified, not assumed: both keys read back as secretKeyRef with no plaintext credential left on the service; /health 200; the emergency poller returned 200 on every tick from 20:23:01 onward (four seconds after the new revision started) and /invariants 200 — a broken token would have 404’d, and a broken Notion token would have surfaced there. Zero errors in the logs since the cutover.

GET /v1/code/triggers is real (it 401s cleanly on a bad token under both Authorization: Bearer and x-api-key) but undocumented, and the project’s anthropic-api-key workspace key is refused by it — with and without the anthropic-beta: experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01 header the sibling /fire endpoint requires.     The tempting wrong answer: the local Claude Code credential is a user OAuth token in the macOS Keychain, and it would probably work. It is not going into Cloud Run — it is user-scoped and it expires, so the runtime sense would go blind at an unannounced future date without saying so. That is the exact failure mode this watchdog exists to catch; building it that way would be self-defeating.

    Consequence: the runtime sense stays exclusive to the LLM Sentinel lane, whose Claude_Code_Remote connector (scoped list_triggers) is the only working door to the scheduler’s record. That is now the load-bearing reason not to retire that lane — recorded in RUNTIMES.md so a future session does not cheerfully delete it. The larger goal still landed, though: the LLM lane stopped duplicating the heartbeat math when it became an auditor on 2026-08-27, which was the expensive half. Each was empty-room-wont-cool fired on a room sitting AT its setpoint (25.23 vs COOL 25.30; twice 23.24 vs COOL 23.05) — flat, empty, HVAC cooling, which is every literal condition canon step 7a lists. The LLM lane declined all three and wrote down why in the Thermal Log: “Step 7a requires flat/rising ambient WHILE failing to reach setpoint”. Readings now match on the Entry title SDM reading — . Canon step 2 updated. Self-limiting (it dies with the LLM lane) but it was corrupting the very comparison shadow exists to produce.

    • Audit. It still computes the whole fleet’s health independently — an auditor that trusts what it audits is worthless — then compares against the sweep’s ALARMS: ledger.     • Runtime watch. Unchanged and still exclusive: the sweep has no trigger-API token, so it is blind to whether each bot’s timer is actually switched on.

Both were wrong: qa-review's own log shows an unbroken hourly run 🕒 00:00 … 🕒 21:00, including 20:00 — nine minutes before the alarm — and the deterministic sweep said all clear at every pass.

    The cause is subtler than a page size. The prompt read the reports through a view sorted by Started At, 40 rows, has_more: true. A rolling daily report is started once at 04:00 but edited every hour — so as the day fills with newer runs it sinks below the cut while its heartbeat is minutes old. The Sentinel never saw the current report, found a stale one from five days earlier, and did the arithmetic on that. A first fix that merely raised the page to 100 was wrong too: a bigger page only moves the cut. v3.2 sorts by the field actually being measured — Last Edited, via SQL, never the view — fetches rolling reports by title, and requires a targeted per-run query to confirm every candidate before it counts. Plus a smell test: an hourly lane reported 117 hours late is presumptively a bad read, because nobody misses five days of an hourly job unnoticed.

    The agreement record is the point. Every pass logs audit: AGREE or a disagreement, so the decision to eventually switch the LLM lane off rests on evidence rather than nerve. Known gap, written into the prompt: the auditor sleeps 23:00–07:00 Toronto while the sweep runs on, so a sweep death overnight is not caught until the 07:00 pass.

    The hole. Every watcher on this fleet asked one question — “was a report filed?” — and that question is forgeable. From 2026-08-22 to 08-25 the Concierge’s cloud trigger was disabled (~21 missed fires) while a Codex fallback kept filing The Concierge — Rolling Daily reports under the same persona name. The Sentinel and The Watchman both ran, both stayed green, and both were correct. “The Concierge” was a persona label, not a runtime, so nothing on the board could tell a live lane from a dead one wearing its name.

    The fix. 🚥 Run Monitor gains three columns — Runtime (the trig_… id, or gha: for GitHub Actions lanes), Runtime state, Runtime checked — and every Live row is now stamped with the thing that actually fires it. The Sentinel (sentinel-v2-2026-08-25) gains §2b: one read-only list_triggers call per pass against the scheduler’s own record, which no agent can fake by writing a report. Disabled, deleted, or a next_run_at stuck in the past → SMS + Sweep Feedback, deduped separately from heartbeat misses and explicitly exempt from the §3a body cross-check — a heartbeat gap is an inference that can be wrong, a disabled trigger is ground truth. It fires even when the heartbeat is green; that pairing is the loudest thing it can say, because it means something other than the intended runtime is filing that lane’s reports.

    Two traps found by probing rather than assuming (🧪 Runner Capability Probe, repurposed — still disabled, manual-run only). Both are written into §2b so they are never rediscovered: (a) the cloud list_triggers route omits enabled when it is false rather than sending false — 21 routines, 19 true, and the 2 with the key absent were exactly the 2 disabled ones. Any watcher reading absent as “unknown, skip” is blind to precisely what it exists to catch. (b) the listing paginates and truncates silently — the desktop API route returned 20 with has_more=true and accepts no cursor, while the cloud route with limit:100 returns all 21 in one page. A dead trigger past the cut would have been invisible forever.

    Privilege, deliberately narrow. The Sentinel had no runtime visibility at all (Notion + Phone.com only), so it gained the Claude_Code_Remote connector — scoped permitted_tools: ["list_triggers"] and verified on read-back. An unattended watchdog that could disable production triggers is a worse problem than the one being solved; it can read the roster and shout, nothing more. If a runtime is off on purpose, the fix is a human setting that row to Paused.

    Still open. The two GitHub Actions lanes (qa-review, watchlist-refresh) are ticked by cron-job.org and this API cannot see them — marked N/A, still heartbeat-only. The Analyst is resolved: its runtime was never missing, only invisible — it was the one routine past the pagination cut. The Sentinel’s first §2b pass named it on sight (trig_01JDu3k596RWLPRvdnBqoG45, enabled, fires ~04:06 Toronto), which is the whole point of asking the scheduler instead of inferring. Worth recording that the row had been marked “unknown, not proven absent” rather than “has no runtime” — the stronger claim would have been wrong. Verified live 02:08Z: 13/13 checkable triggers stamped Live, no Sweep Feedback row, no SMS, and the pass logged all clear (runtimes 13/13) — the count is deliberate, since silence cannot prove §2b ran.

A backstop that disappears under load is not a backstop.

    Symptom: phonecom-mcp tools returned Phone.com API 401: token invalid/revoked while the token in ~/.env authenticated against api.phone.com/v4/accounts with HTTP 200.     Cause: canon’s §3 runbook ended with a bare gcloud run services update phonecom-mcp --region … with no flags. That exits ERROR: (gcloud.run.services.update) No configuration change requested and mints no revision. The secret is bound as secretKeyRef: key: latest, so a new version is only picked up by a new revision — the service went on serving version 1, which had been disabled. Three of the four stores were current and the one that serves traffic was not.

    Fix: the command now carries a churn value — --update-env-vars COLD_START=$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M) — which forces a revision without changing behaviour. Rotation completed across all four stores: ~/.env, GitHub Actions secret, Secret Manager version 3, and Cloud Run revision phonecom-mcp-00007-5n7. list_sms verified live afterwards. Canon patched at CREDENTIALS.md §3, commit f18020d3.

    The second rule added to canon: verify before rotating. The instinct on a 401 is to mint a new token, and it is usually wrong — curl the API with the existing one first. Rotating a working credential turns a one-place problem into a four-place problem, and the panel’s regenerate button issues short-lived tokens that expire within hours (the cause of the 2026-07-17 SMS outage), so a reflex rotation can also seed the next failure.

    Also found, unfixed: list_sms accepts direction: "in" and returns outbound messages anyway — the filter is not applied server-side. Anything relying on it is reading the wrong set. Not blocking, but it silently widens every caller’s result.

    Why this class of failure hides: each store reports success on its own write, and nothing compares what the running revision is actually serving against what the stores hold. The 401 is loud, but it points at the credential — the last place worth looking.

The killed pass had written partially, which is harmless here: every write is idempotent and fill-only, and the next complete pass re-derives the whole board from scratch. Nothing wrong was written; it was incomplete, not corrupt. No messages went out — confirmations queue at Pending Review regardless.

    900s is a tuning fix, not a repair. The sweep reads the board one day at a time — 15 sequential round-trips across the 14-day horizon before it touches a single booking — so duration scales with the board and the board grows. The true ceiling is 1800s no matter what the timeout says, because the job runs every 30 minutes: past that, passes overlap, and overlap breaks single-writer, the constraint 079 learned from the Codex collision (two actors on one instruction, each verifying its own write as correct, nothing detecting it). Ticket 087 carries the real fix: ask for a date range, which /bookingslists already accepts.

    Considered and declined: shrinking the horizon to 7 days would have halved the reads tonight, but bookings 8–14 days out would then get no prerequisites until they drifted closer. That is seeing less, not going faster.

    The lesson worth keeping: two limits set to the same number is not two safety nets, it is one. And a dry run is not a timing test for a lane that writes.

    The Gmail ledger poller only ever looked forward, so any message it missed once was missed forever — it now re-scans a week, dailyFIX

    The failure mode, stated plainly: gmail_pull.py lists with after:{cursor - 3600} and then advances the cursor past everything it saw. A message that was invisible at poll time — quarantined in spam is the leading candidate — is skipped, and the skip is permanent: a human clicking “Not spam” an hour later changes nothing, because the cursor has already moved past that hour. Found on Camille Quesada’s 2026-08-06 19:32Z booking mail (ticket 067): Junyan’s reply reached canon, her question never did, so the thread reads as the desk writing to her unprompted. Every other turn across Aug 5–7 was present. This was not the outage — the cursor rides in the same commit as the messages, so an outage-lost message re-captures on the next tick. This one was skipped.

    The repair fixes the class, not the instance. Once every 24h the poller re-lists the last 7 days with the same query and writes whatever canon is missing. It heals any kind of skip — spam, an API blip, a mid-page failure, a delivery whose internalDate lands behind the cursor — not just the one that was found.

    includeSpamTrash deliberately stays false. This is the design decision worth remembering: mail still sitting in spam is spam and stays out of the ledger, and a human clicking “Not spam” is the repair — the next re-scan sees it and files it. Flipping the flag would have bought the same recovery plus a second exclusion list to keep correct forever.

    Three properties designed for, then tested. The re-scan never moves the forward cursor (it reads old mail by definition; letting it touch last_epoch would be a way to skip live mail — the defect, rebuilt). It is loud: a recovery prints ::warning:: with the count, because a re-scan that healed quietly would hide the fact that the forward pass has a blind spot. And it is nearly free — the existing one-tree-scan have set means an already-captured message costs a dict lookup and no messages.get call, so a week of re-listing is a handful of list calls and zero writes in steady state.

    ✓ Proved by running it, not by reasoning. A message three days old and far behind the cursor was deleted from canon; the forward pass correctly did not see it, the re-scan recovered it byte-identical and said so, and last_epoch was untouched. The 24h gate held on an immediate re-run; a forced re-scan in steady state wrote nothing. dc-canon 8e79f74e.

    Two things learned on the way, both worth keeping. A spam round-trip is label-destructive — marking a live message SPAM and removing SPAM stripped IMPORTANT and CATEGORY_*, leaving only user labels — so labels can never serve as evidence of a message’s spam history; the trace is erased by the rescue itself. And the business Gmail connector can trash but cannot untrash (untrash_message → “The caller does not have permission”); removing the TRASH label directly works.

    The Skedda anti-forgery token was outliving its own session, and every read went anonymousFIX

    The token is minted FOR a session, but the cache was a bare process global. When the cookie rotated underneath it, a warm Cloud Run instance kept presenting the old token — and Skedda answered HTTP 200 with the holders stripped. Not an error, not a 401: real-looking bookings with price 0, payment_status 0, user null, title null. Nothing raised, so nothing noticed. This is the same anonymous-read signature that cost the fleet a day on 08-11, arriving by a different door.

    Fixed in services/event-gate/skedda_read.py: the cache is keyed on a sha256 fingerprint of the cookie that produced the token, so a rotation invalidates it automatically, and carries a 15-minute TTL (SKEDDA_TOKEN_TTL) so no token can outlive its session in a long-warm instance. reset_session_cache() drops the token and the space-name cache together; the 401/403 path calls it instead of half-clearing. The fingerprint is deliberately not the cookie — that value ends up in comparisons and, one careless log line later, in Cloud Logging.

    The stripped read now self-heals. The Registrar drops the cached session and reads once more before giving up, so a stale token repairs itself inside the same pass with no human involved. A second stripped read still fails loudly and files sweep-blind — the retry must not paper over a genuinely non-admin cookie, which is a different fault with a different fix. Six new tests: rotation forces a re-scrape, a stable cookie does not, TTL expiry, the retry, the retry not hiding a real failure, and the fingerprint never leaking the cookie. Suite 397.

At one-minute cadence that is ~1,440 logins a day against a provider that locks accounts for repeated authentication — and the token died twice on 2026-08-12 while several surfaces were logging in independently.

    Now: one session, reused. Warm calls run 0.83s. Re-login happens only on session death or after six hours, and exactly once — never in a loop, because a lockout costs the whole system while a missed tick costs sixty seconds. Non-session errors never trigger a retry, so a write that failed mid-flight is never blindly re-run.

    Everything downstream of alarm-mcp gets faster for free, including the presence gate's /panel-states call.

  • 2026-08-13

    The panel can now say "the siren is sounding"SIGNAL

    Partitions previously reported one flag, faulted, which was true for a low battery, a propped door, a broken sensor and an active alarm alike. Right question for the morning check; useless for anything that acts. Automation keyed to it would have disarmed the studios over a dying battery.

    in_alarm is now its own field, meaning only that the siren is going off. faulted is unchanged, so nothing downstream shifted.

    Still unproven: nothing has tripped since, so in_alarm has never been observed true. A deliberate trip on 693 is pending — that single test decides whether the whole watchdog design holds.

    The registry claimed a twice-daily trigger (0 8,10 UTC), branching on the hour: 04:00 for the overnight arm-check that inherited the retired Closer's job, ~06:00 for the access preflight. The live trigger reads 0 10 — a single fire.

    So the morning preflight has been running and the 04:00 "are the empty studios armed" pass has not, for an unknown stretch. Restoring it is a deliberate decision, not a silent fix. (Resolved same night — see the FIX entry above.)

    Panel control landed 2026-08-11 — arm_alarm, disarm_alarm, panel_state — but README-gcp.md still promised "read-only by construction, the package has no arm/disarm/lock calls." Anyone judging how much to trust the service got a wrong answer from its own documentation.

    Corrected, along with a retracted theory in the provision route that blamed vanishing access windows on timestamp seconds. Both now state plainly that they were wrong, rather than quietly reading correctly — the failure worth remembering is that the docs kept vouching for a guarantee the code had dropped.

    Connectors cache their tool lists. A redeploy alone will not surface a new tool; the connector has to reconnect.
